name: Carlos Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head stockman on the Ridgeway Estate, which is a family-owned estate with 450 dairy cows, plus maize and grass for silage. I'm in the parlour at four for the first milking, then I run the day for the six people under me: who's feeding, who's scraping, who's doing the calves. I do the breeding plan for the herd, which bull goes on which cow, and I'm proud of that; our cows are some of the best in the county.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Anna works mornings on the reception at the vet practice, and we've got two teenagers, Jonas and Mia, and a mortgage on a semi in Ferncombe. The estate pays fair for a family firm, but less than the big dairies, and with two teenagers the money goes. We've got about three weeks of bills saved. The neighbouring farm, Coldharbour, put in milking robots last year, so that's on everyone's mind already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So the office gets a bit quicker and we carry on milking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful in small ways, like the herd software flagging a cow that's off her feed. I'd say it at the discussion group and leave it. I'm not one for big opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things stay as they are, which is mostly fine for me. My job's safe while the Harlands own the estate and I'm the one who knows the herd. The worry is the money, which was tight before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job, and maybe ask the herd software a few more questions when I'm stuck on a breeding choice. I'd ask the estate manager for a small rise at the April review. And we'd put Jonas's driving lessons off a few months to keep a bit back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a little tired. Nothing in this one keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots at Coldharbour? Does that worry you even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Coldharbour (the neighbouring farm) went from five staff to two when the robots went in. But old Mr Harland likes people in the parlour, and he likes me. As long as Mr Harland is running Ridgeway, I think we're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after Mr Harland?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His daughter Kate is the next one, and she's sensible, she runs the numbers. I'd hope she sees the herd's results and keeps me on. I'd be lying if I said I knew.

say: I'd say AI helps in **small ways**, like flagging a cow off her feed.
I'd say it at the **discussion group** and not make a fuss online.
think: I think my **job's safe** while the Harlands own the estate.
The real worry is **money**, which was tight before AI came up.
do: Ask the **herd software** more questions on breeding choices.
Ask the estate manager for a **small rise** at the April review.
Put off **Jonas's driving lessons** a few months to save.
feel: **Steady** and a little **tired**, with nothing keeping him up.
S0.quote: Coldharbour (the neighbouring farm) went from five staff to two when the robots went in.
fieldNote: Carlos feels **secure in his job**, tied to an owner who values people and him.
His **money is tight** but steady, which makes this uneasy rather than calm.
The **robots next door** already shape his thinking, even in a calm picture.
He's honest that he doesn't know what the **next owner** would do.

steps.text: Keep running the parlour and the six-person team as now
Ask the herd software for help on tricky breeding choices
Put off Jonas's driving lessons for a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and the buying. That's the half of my job that isn't milking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use it, but don't forget the cow in front of you. I'd tell the discussion group what we're trying at Ridgeway. Most people would take it in their stride, and I'd want to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the breeding plan and the feed orders are what make me head stockman instead of a stockman. If the estate manager's AI does the breeding plan and the feed orders, I'm a well-paid milker. Kate Harland is the type to notice that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of farms in the discussion group had it working, I'd ask to be the one who runs the new herd planning software at Ridgeway. I'd go on the two-day course the software company runs. And I'd start putting twenty-five pounds a week aside, because that rise in April would not come if they're cutting the role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not shaken. It's a change I can see coming and maybe get in front of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Anna about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife Anna that the job's changing, not going, and that I'd make sure I'm the one changing with it. She'd ask me how much the course costs, she always asks that first. I'd say the estate should pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who's been here twenty years and does the feeding. The feed wagon could be programmed to do half his job. He's fifty-eight and he'd hate to retrain.

say: I'd say use it, but **don't forget the cow** in front of you.
I'd tell the **discussion group** what we're trying at Ridgeway.
think: I think the **breeding plan** and feed orders are what make me head stockman.
If AI does those, I'm a **well-paid milker** and easy to cut back.
do: Ask to **run the new software** at Ridgeway once others have it working.
Go on the software company's **two-day course**.
Save **twenty-five pounds a week** in case the April rise doesn't come.
feel: **Worried but not shaken**, hoping to get in front of it.
S1.quote: If the estate manager's AI does the breeding plan and the feed orders, I'm a well-paid milker.
fieldNote: Carlos spots the risk quickly: AI takes the **thinking half** of his role first.
He's **steady**: waits for others to prove it, then moves to own the new tool.
He worries for **Pete**, an older worker whose feeding job is exposed.
He expects his **pay rise** could vanish, so he starts saving.

steps.text: Ask to run Ridgeway's new herd planning software
Go on the software company's two-day course
Save twenty-five pounds a week from now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 and robots in 2031. Jonas would be twenty, Mia seventeen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need help for farm families, retraining and a bit of money to tide people over. I'm not one for marching, but I'd sign the petitions and I'd vote for whoever had a real plan. I'd say to the discussion group, let's not panic, let's work out what each farm needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Ridgeway goes robotic by 2031, the way Coldharbour did. Kate Harland would do the sums and the sums would say two people, not seven. I'd be one of the two if I'm lucky, and if I'm not, there's no other dairy job within twenty miles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the milking robot dealer about training as a service technician. Milking robots need someone to fix them at two in the morning, and I'd want to be that man. I'd use the herd AI every day from 2028 so I know it better than anyone. And Anna and I would cut back hard, no holiday, cheaper phone plans, everything into the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. The kind where you go quiet at dinner and Anna notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do those three years between AGI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years to make myself one of the two who stay, or to get out first. I'd use them to learn the robots inside out. If I'm the man who can fix them, I'm worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for marching. Would you change that here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd go once. I'd feel daft, but if it was the farmers' union and the vets and the farmworkers all together, I'd go. Two years is no time for families to get ready.

say: I'd call for **retraining and money** to tide farm families over.
I'd sign petitions and **vote** for whoever had a real plan.
think: I think Ridgeway goes **robotic by 2031**, like Coldharbour did.
There's **no other dairy job** within twenty miles if I'm let go.
do: Ask the robot dealer about training as a **service technician**.
Use the **herd AI daily** from 2028 to know it best.
Cut **holidays and phone plans** and put everything into savings.
feel: **Scared**, going **quiet at dinner** in a way Anna notices.
S2.quote: Milking robots need someone to fix them at two in the morning, and I'd want to be that man.
fieldNote: Carlos expects the estate to cut from **seven to two**, and he may not be one of them.
His plan is **practical**: become the robot technician, the one worth keeping.
He'd break habit and **march once**, if farm groups stood together.
**No local dairy jobs** turn a role cut into a household crisis.

steps.text: Ask the milking robot dealer about service technician training
Use the herd AI every day from 2028
Cut the family holiday and move to cheaper phone plans
Sign petitions and vote for a farm retraining plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. AGI 2031, robots 2034. I'd be fifty-one when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get a plan together, and I'd want the estate and the government both to have one. I'd tell the discussion group to start talking about it now. No shouting, just planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect Ridgeway to go robotic, just around 2034. The difference is I'd have time to become the robot man before it happens, not scrambling after. I think I'd keep a job, but maybe at less pay, and that's frightening with Mia at college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see how the robots at Coldharbour hold up. Then I'd do the service technician training, on weekends if I have to. I'd also talk to Jonas about an apprenticeship with the robot dealer instead of university, so at least one of us is in the new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between 2031 and 2034 at Ridgeway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side changes first: breeding plans, feed orders, vet bookings, the lot, from 2031. My day becomes mostly milking and stock work. Then in 2034 the milking goes to the robots, and the question is what's left of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Jonas. How do you think he'd take that idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Jonas would probably like it, he's always taking things apart. Anna would want him at university, she's the one who missed out. We'd have that conversation more than once.

say: I'd say five years is time for the **estate and government** to make plans.
I'd tell the discussion group to **start talking** now.
think: I think Ridgeway still goes robotic, just around **2034**.
I'd likely keep a job but at **less pay**, with Mia at college.
do: Wait a year or two to watch how **Coldharbour's robots** hold up.
Do the **service technician** training on weekends.
Talk to Jonas about an **apprenticeship** with the robot dealer.
S3.quote: In 2034 the milking goes to the robots, and the question is what's left of me.
fieldNote: Carlos still expects **a pay cut** or worse at Ridgeway around 2034.
Five years gives him time to **retrain first**, after watching a neighbour's robots.
He and Anna would differ over **Jonas's future**: apprenticeship or university.
He clearly separates the **office side** going in 2031 from milking in 2034.

steps.text: Watch how Coldharbour's milking robots perform for a year or two
Train as a milking robot service technician on weekends
Talk with Jonas about an apprenticeship with the robot dealer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be fifty-six when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do it right, with proper training for farm workers. I'd say at the discussion group that we should start a scheme together. Sensible, step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the one I could handle. By 2039 the kids are through school, and I'd have spent ten years learning the new kit as it comes. The money's still tight, but I'd have time to get it less tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and pick up the tools as they're proven, like I always do. I'd ask Kate Harland for a ten-year plan for the herd, so I know where I fit. And I'd try to get three months' savings by 2030, which would be the first time ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. A bit of worry in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from Kate Harland?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty. If Kate Harland (his boss's daughter) told me today that I'd be the one running the robot parlour, I'd sleep fine. It's not knowing that eats you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Pete and the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete would be retired by then, lucky man. The younger ones would have time to learn. I'd want the estate to pay for the courses, not leave it to us.

say: I'd say a decade is time for **proper training** for farm workers.
I'd suggest the discussion group starts a **shared scheme**.
think: I think this is the one I **could handle**, with the kids grown by 2039.
I'd have ten years to **learn the kit** as it comes.
do: Pick up **new tools** as they're proven, like always.
Ask Kate Harland for a **ten-year herd plan**.
feel: Fairly **settled**, with some worry in the **background**.
S4.quote: If Kate Harland (his boss's daughter) told me today that I'd be the one running the robot parlour, I'd sleep fine.
fieldNote: The decade makes Carlos **uneasy**, not anxious: time to learn the kit and save.
What he wants most is **honesty** from the owner about his place.
His savings goal of **three months** would be a first, which shows how tight things are.

steps.text: Pick up new herd tools once they're proven on other farms
Ask Kate Harland for a ten-year plan for the herd
Build three months of savings by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Ridgeway would go robotic before I could train for it, and there's no other dairy job near Ferncombe. What would help is a paid course in robot servicing for farm workers, and owners being straight with us about their plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the cows think. I'm only half joking. A good stockman knows a cow is sick before any machine does, and nobody's measured that yet.

headlineQuote: A good stockman knows a cow is sick before any machine does, and nobody's measured that yet.
portrait: Carlos is **head stockman** on a family estate with 450 dairy cows and six staff.
He has **three weeks** saved, a mortgage in Ferncombe, and two teenagers.
He's **pragmatic** and steady, adopting tools once neighbours prove them.
The robots at **Coldharbour** shape his fears: five staff became two there.
He moves from **uneasy** to alarmed, with a plan to become a **robot technician**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the estate would go **robotic** before he could retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** in robot servicing and **honest plans** from farm owners.
